title: Ecommerce Development Social Content: 30-Day Plan
description: A social content plan for an ecommerce development brand: Instagram, LinkedIn, and repurposing strategy to distribute your topical cluster content to a wider audience.

ogDescription: How to repurpose the content cluster into Instagram carousels, LinkedIn posts, and short-form video that actually drive traffic and leads.

This page is the operating plan. It covers what to post on each platform, how to repurpose each cluster page into specific post types, a 30-day calendar, and the performance signals to watch. It assumes you have already published the cluster (Days 1–21 of the roadmap). If you have not, publish first — social amplifies existing content, it does not replace it.

The most common mistake with social content for a service business is treating it as a separate content operation. The result is two parallel content streams that do not reinforce each other — SEO content nobody sees because it is not promoted, and social content that does not accumulate authority because it lives and dies in the feed.

The correct approach is the reverse: build the cluster once, then carve it into social posts that drive readers back to the full pages. Every social post is a preview of a page. The page is the destination, not the social post.

Social distribution does not build an audience from zero; it amplifies existing authority to people who already have some interest.
Social reach is temporary; search rankings compound. Social supports SEO, not the other way around.
This is organic distribution. Paid social is a separate decision with different economics.

blocks.text: Why this works for a service business

inline: B2B service buyers, especially in ecommerce, are highly engaged on LinkedIn and increasingly on Instagram. They follow agencies and developers they are considering hiring, and they read posts that speak directly to their concerns. A post like "5 signs your ecommerce developer is not really an ecommerce developer" reaches exactly the audience you want — founders and marketing leads evaluating developers — and it is directly sourced from

The social post does not need to be brilliant. It needs to be specific, useful, and clearly linked to a deeper page. That is achievable with a one-page plan per post, and it is how most successful B2B service brands operate on social.
Not every platform is worth the effort. For an ecommerce development brand, the following platforms matter and the following do not.

blocks.text: How to produce this in one sitting

inline: The calendar above should take

to produce, not 30. Open each source page, extract the relevant snippet, write a hook, note the format, and paste the link. For carousels, write the 6–10 slide titles at the same time. For reels, write the 15–30 second script at the same time. Do not try to produce social content day by day — batch it.

blocks.text: What to do with the batching output

items: using a tool like Buffer, Hootsuite, or Later. The point of the calendar is that you do not have to think about it again for 30 days.

b: Do not schedule the carousel graphics without producing them.

items: Carousels require design, not just text. If you do not have a designer, use Canva templates — the visual quality matters less than the content quality for this audience.
Keep 2–3 slots per month for reactive posts (industry news, a new case study, a response to something happening in the ecommerce world). The calendar is a floor, not a ceiling.

inline: Repurposing is not copying. A good repurposed post changes the format, the length, and the framing — it does not just paste the source paragraph into a social post.

items: A 400-word section becomes a 100-word post or a 10-slide carousel. Never a 400-word post.
A question becomes a list of "what a strong answer sounds like." A red flag becomes "5 signs you are about to be ghosted." A case study result becomes "how we cut load time in half in 9 weeks."
Start with the specific moment the reader is in, not the general topic. Not "ecommerce developer vetting" but "you are on the third sales call and still not sure."

b: Add one thing that is not on the page.

items: A personal aside, a more specific number, a "what I would do if I were you" line. The post should feel like it was written for the platform, not extracted from the page.

blocks.text: How to keep the source pages and the social posts in sync

inline: Every social post should link to the specific cluster page it comes from. When a page is updated, the social posts that point to it still work — they do not need to be updated. This is why social is distribution, not production: the source pages live and evolve independently, and social posts are cheap pointers to them.

Social is harder to measure than SEO, because the attribution is indirect and the time lag is longer. But there are four metrics that actually matter for this strategy, and three that look like they matter but do not.

items: Not impressions, not likes — actual clicks to the source pages. Use UTM parameters on every link.

b: Time on page for social-sourced traffic.

items: If readers land on the cluster page and leave in 10 seconds, the post was misleading. If they spend 2+ minutes, the post was a good teaser.
The percentage of social-sourced visitors who request a quote, download the brief template, or contact you.
"I saw your post about X" is a direct signal that the post reached a real buyer.
Impressions measure reach, not interest. A post with 50,000 impressions and 3 clicks is worse than a post with 500 impressions and 20 clicks.
A growing follower count is nice, but for a B2B service business, it is not the metric that predicts revenue.
Likes are a weak signal because they are easy to give and do not correlate with buying intent. Comment quality matters more than comment count.
Use utm_source (linkedin / instagram), utm_medium (social), and utm_campaign (the source page slug). This lets you attribute traffic and conversions to specific posts.
Set up conversion events for quote requests, brief template downloads, and contact form submissions. Segment by UTM source.

Every Monday, review the previous week's posts: which posts drove clicks, which pages got the most time-on-page, and which posts generated the highest conversion rate. Adjust the next week's calendar accordingly.

blocks.text: What to do if the numbers are flat

inline: If after 30 days the click-throughs are minimal, the problem is almost always one of three things: (1) the hooks are not specific enough, (2) the posts are too generic, or (3) the audience on the platform is not the right audience for this topic. Do not add more posts — fix the hooks and the framing first. One specific post that generates 50 clicks is worth more than 30 generic posts that generate none.

sections.title: What Not to Do on Social

inline: These are the patterns that waste the most effort and produce the least return for a B2B service brand.
"5 tips for a better ecommerce store" is generic. "The one question that catches 90% of bad developers" is specific. Generic advice is easy to scroll past; specific advice is hard to ignore.

blocks.text: Do not post without a specific CTA

inline: Every post should end with a clear next step. "Let me know what you think" is not a CTA. "The full 26-question checklist is linked in the comments" is a CTA.

The "what didn't go to plan" content from the case study is the highest-engagement content on your site, because most agencies post only wins. Post the failure stories. They build more trust than the success stories do.

blocks.text: Do not treat Instagram as a portfolio

inline: Instagram is not a gallery of your best work. It is a channel for teaching, opinion, and insight. Portfolio work belongs on
, not in a carousel.

blocks.text: Do not use TikTok for this topic

inline: Your CSV data confirms this: every TikTok query related to ecommerce website developer has zero volume, and the ones that exist are navigational (e.g., "ecommerce website developer 1"). There is no meaningful audience for this topic on TikTok, and the effort-to-return ratio is poor. Skip it.

blocks.text: Do not post on a schedule that you cannot maintain

inline: 1 post per day on LinkedIn and 3–4 posts per week on Instagram is a sustainable schedule for a small team. 3 posts per day is not. The calendar above is designed to be sustainable, not impressive. A sustainable schedule that lasts 6 months beats an aggressive schedule that collapses after 3 weeks.

faqs.q: Do I need to be on every platform?
a: No. LinkedIn and Instagram are the two that matter for this topic. Everything else is optional, and TikTok is a skip. Focus your effort on the two channels that reach buyers, and ignore the ones that do not.

faqs.q: How long before social starts driving traffic?
a: If the cluster is already published and indexed, social can start driving traffic within the first week. Real measurable lift — a steady flow of social-sourced visitors to specific pages — usually takes 30 to 60 days of consistent posting. Expecting faster results is the most common reason social programs get abandoned.

faqs.q: Should I post the same content on LinkedIn and Instagram?
a: Same core idea, different format. A LinkedIn carousel is not the same as an Instagram carousel, and a LinkedIn text post is not the same as an Instagram reel. The source is the same; the format adapts to the platform.

faqs.q: How much time does this take per week?
a: If the calendar is produced once per month (one working day), the weekly effort is roughly 1–2 hours for scheduling, engagement, and comments. Producing content daily — rather than batching — multiplies that time by 4–5x and usually leads to burnout.

faqs.q: Do I need a designer to produce carousels?
a: No, but the carousels should not look sloppy. Canva templates designed for B2B content are sufficient. What matters more than design is the content: the hook, the one idea per slide, and the specific CTA.

faqs.q: What if I hate social media?
a: Then do not do it. Social is a distribution channel, not a moral requirement. If you have the cluster, the pillar, and the internal linking right, SEO alone can generate meaningful traffic and leads. Social amplifies existing authority; it does not create it. If you would rather spend the effort on more cluster pages or a stronger case study, that is a reasonable choice.

faqs.q: How does this connect back to the SEO roadmap?
a: Every post links to a cluster page, which builds internal page authority through engagement signals and (indirectly) through brand searches. The SEO roadmap is the source of truth; social is the amplifier. If a post performs well, it is a signal that the source page has strong hooks — which is useful information for optimizing the page itself.

faqs.q: What is the single most important post to get right?
a: The first post. If the first post performs well, it establishes momentum for the calendar. If it does not, fix the hook and try again before moving on. Do not run a full 30-day calendar with a hook that has already been proven weak.

inline: Batch-produce the 30 days of content in one sitting, schedule it, and then spend your weekly social time on engagement and comments — not on production. The calendar above is a floor, not a ceiling: leave room for reactive posts and for the posts that surprise you by performing well.
